scope: Hodgson-linked transfers of Nepal/Himalayan paper pulp, now including recipient identity control and district transport-infrastructure context.
central_claim: The 25 March 1842 twenty-four-package pulp shipment was routed through a Chumparun joint-magistrate forwarding node operating in a corridor with strongly seasonal road constraints and multimodal land/water options. The most probable recipient was Edward E. Woodcock, appointed to Chumparun on 8 February 1842, despite Regmi's transcript reading 'G. Woodcock'. Actual route, freight cost, Calcutta receiver and relation to Serampore remain unresolved.

shipments.control: outer packaging and detailed transit route unresolved

shipments.recipient_transcript_exact: G. Woodcock Esq., Joint Magistrate, Champaun
recipient_evidence: Bengal and Agra Directory 1844: Edward E. Woodcock, joint magistrate and deputy collector of Chumparun, 8 February 1842
Bengal Directory 1840: Edward E. Woodcock at Balasore from 12 February 1839
no competing G. Woodcock recovered in the Chumparun joint-magistrate office for March 1842

infrastructure_context.source: Robert Rankine, Notes on the Medical Topography of the Districts of Sarun, report dated 22 Jan 1838, printed Calcutta 1839
observations: Great and Little Gunduck navigable for small boats through the year, but Great Gunduck navigation difficult and dry-season capacity reduced in places to very small boats
bad-road remarks explicitly extended to Govind Gunge and Bettiah roads
high road to Chumparun via Sutter Ghat hardly passable in many places for five or six months of the year
bridges urgently required for wheeled-carriage access during rainy season
neglected cross roads could force produce transport by human head-load for about six months, increasing expense
infrastructure_context.use_rule: context for route feasibility and freight cost only; does not establish actual pulp route or carrier mode

source_control_rules: Preserve G. Woodcock as the exact Regmi transcript reading.
Use Edward E. Woodcock as probable normalization only until original Bihar State Archives initials are read.
Do not turn Rankine's general human-carriage observation into a claim that the pulp packages were carried by coolies.
Do not infer package weight from Rankine's twenty-seer load example.
Keep Govind Gang and Govind Gunge exact strings separate pending historical geographic normalization.
Keep both Hodgson route alternatives live.
Do not connect the consignment directly to Serampore without receipt/forwarding evidence.
